newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Former warlord threatens to sue, denies war crimes.
newsitem.headline: Former warlord threatens to sue, denies war crimes.

text.p: Former Serbian warlord Zeljko Raznatovic denied on Wednesday he had ever committed war crimes and said he would sue an American television network for alleging he was responsible for atrocities in Croatia and Bosnia.

"I have been charged, tried and sentenced by the CNN. Does CNN have a jail of its own?" Raznatovic, better known as Arkan, told a news conference in Belgrade, responding to allegations in a recent CNN story "Wanted".
"I have been investigated by the prosecutor's office of the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague ... I have not been indicted for any war crime," Arkan said.
His foreign policy adviser Giovanni Di Stefano said he had received a letter from the war crimes tribunal in The Hague informing him that Arkan was not on a list of indictees.
The tribunal has indicted 75 people for war crimes of whom only nine are in custody.
In December 1991, the former United States secretary of state, Lawrence Eagleburger, described Arkan as a suspected war criminal.
Former U.S. peace mediator Richard Holbrooke said in the CNN story that Arkan must be brought to justice.

"The man is almost certainly a hands-on murderer. His public display of freedom sends a signal to everyone else that you can get away with this kind of thing. Arkan must be brought to justice," he said.

The CNN story coincides with a visit to the Balkans by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to press home the importance of implementing the Dayton peace accord and handing over indicted war criminals to The Hague.
"To Western governents Arkan is a murderous thug -- The most prominent instrument of ethnic cleansing in Croatia and Bosnia," the CNN report said.
State Department spokesman Nick Burns told reporters that Albright had pressed Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to try Arkan in Yugoslavia.
"We think he played a very negative role (in the war)," Burns said.
But Arkan said he was just defending his own people against Moslems and Croats and described CNN as a tool for exerting political pressure on Milosevic.
Arkan set up his notorious Tigers militia shortly after war broke out in Croatia in August 1991.
He has denied accusations that the well-equipped paramilitaries, based in Erdut, northern Croatia, played a prominent role in besieging and looting the Croatian town of Vukovar in the autumn of 1991.
Despite Arkan's alleged role at Vukovar, the Croatian government has so far not sought to incriminate him in war crimes.
He was caught by Croatian police in 1991 and served six months out of a 20 month sentence for possession of arms but was then handed over to Belgrade authorities.
